subtopic_detail: Inflammatory back pain in a young adult with normal plain radiographs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28 year old man with 10 months of low back and buttock pain. It is worst when he has been still, wakes him in the second half of the night, and eases after he has been moving for half an hour.

He describes about 90 minutes of stiffness each morning. Ibuprofen helps substantially. He has had one episode of a painful red eye treated by an optometrist and his sister has ulcerative colitis. On examination lumbar flexion is reduced with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm and chest expansion is 4 cm, with no neurological deficit and negative straight leg raise. Anteroposterior pelvis and lumbar spine radiographs are reported as normal with no sacroiliac erosion or sclerosis.

data_table.Examination: Modified Schober 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, no neurological deficit, negative straight leg raise
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5); erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (less than 15); pelvis and lumbar spine radiographs reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request human leucocyte antigen B27 testing and manage on that result
options.rationale: The antigen is carried by around 8 per cent of the Australian population and by many people who never develop disease, so it shifts probability but cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis alone (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Repeat the pelvic radiographs in 12 months to look for interval change
options.rationale: Radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear and waiting for it is precisely what produced the historical diagnostic delay of nearly a decade in this disease (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints with a rheumatology referral
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging detects bone marrow oedema in the sacroiliac joints years before radiographic change and is what allows the non radiographic form of axial disease to be diagnosed and treated (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Request computed tomography of the lumbar spine to assess the facet joints
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established bony change well but is insensitive to active inflammation and delivers substantial gonadal radiation to a young man (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Refer for a structured physiotherapy programme without further imaging
options.rationale: Exercise therapy is a mainstay of treatment and will be needed, but starting it without a diagnosis withholds the biologic therapy that changes the disease course in those who fail anti inflammatory treatment (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by onset before 45, duration beyond three months, insidious onset, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, night pain waking the patient, and a good response to anti inflammatory drugs. Recognising the pattern is what separates this from the far commoner mechanical back pain, and the extra articular clues here, a painful red eye suggesting anterior uveitis and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease, add substantially to the probability. Plain radiographs are normal for years in the non radiographic form of axial spondyloarthritis, which affects women as often as men and carries the same symptom burden. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints is therefore the investigation of choice, and it matters because effective treatment exists and delay costs spinal mobility that does not return.
key_points: Night pain that improves with movement is the defining symptom pattern
Anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are associated features
Plain radiographs remain normal for years in early disease
Magnetic resonance imaging shows sacroiliac bone marrow oedema early
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports but does not establish the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about a previous painful red eye, because anterior uveitis occurs in a substantial minority of people with axial spondyloarthritis and is often the only extra articular clue in an otherwise ordinary back pain history.

subtopic_detail: Separating true iron overload from a raised ferritin caused by inflammation or metabolic disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45 year old man of northern European ancestry who came in about tiredness and stiff painful hands. He has had a raised ferritin noted twice over the past year.

He has a body mass index of 32 kg per square metre, treated hypertension and impaired fasting glucose, so the previous doctor attributed the ferritin to fatty liver. He drinks four standard drinks on a Friday night and none otherwise. His father died at 58 of liver disease that the family attributed to drinking. On examination he has tenderness and bony swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands, no jaundice or spider naevi, and a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 138/84, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Bony swelling and tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no jaundice, ascites or spider naevi
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1450 mcg/L (30-300); transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45); alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 45); C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5); glycated haemoglobin 45 mmol/mol (less than 48)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attribute the ferritin to fatty liver and repeat the iron studies in six months
options.rationale: Fatty liver and inflammation raise ferritin as an acute phase protein but leave the transferrin saturation normal or low, and a saturation of 68 per cent indicates genuine iron loading (Source: HSANZ Iron Overload).

options.text: Begin weekly venesection now and monitor the ferritin every four weeks
options.rationale: Venesection is likely to be the treatment, but establishing the genetic diagnosis first determines family testing and the assessment of liver fibrosis that must accompany it (Source: HSANZ Iron Overload).

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy to quantify hepatic iron and assess the degree of fibrosis
options.rationale: Biopsy has been displaced by genetic testing and magnetic resonance quantification for diagnosis, and it is now reserved for staging fibrosis when non invasive assessment is inconclusive (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Advise complete alcohol abstinence and recheck the liver enzymes in three months
options.rationale: Reducing alcohol is worthwhile, but four standard drinks a week does not explain a transferrin saturation of 68 per cent and the delay wastes three months (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Request HFE genotyping and assess the liver for fibrosis non invasively
options.rationale: A raised transferrin saturation with a high ferritin in this ancestry group is the indication for HFE genotyping, and a ferritin above 1000 mcg/L is the threshold at which significant fibrosis becomes likely and must be assessed (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis; HSANZ Iron Overload).

explanation.summary: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so it rises with inflammation, alcohol, malignancy and metabolic liver disease far more often than it rises from iron overload, and the transferrin saturation is what separates these. A saturation above about 45 per cent with a high ferritin points to genuine loading and triggers HFE genotyping, with C282Y homozygosity accounting for the great majority of cases in people of northern European ancestry. The arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is a characteristic early clue that is frequently dismissed as osteoarthritis. A ferritin above 1000 mcg/L predicts advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis, which changes surveillance because established cirrhosis carries an ongoing risk of hepatocellular carcinoma even after iron is removed. First degree relatives are offered testing once the genotype is known, since treatment before organ damage develops gives a normal life expectancy.
key_points: Transferrin saturation separates iron overload from a reactive ferritin rise
HFE genotyping is the diagnostic test in the right ancestry group
Ferritin above 1000 mcg/L predicts significant hepatic fibrosis
Second and third metacarpophalangeal arthropathy is a characteristic clue
Offer testing to first degree relatives once the genotype is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Cirrhosis established before venesection begins does not regress, and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma persists after iron depletion, so those patients need six monthly ultrasound surveillance for life.

subtopic_detail: Who should be screened for intracranial aneurysm in polycystic kidney disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 38 year old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease diagnosed at 30. Her blood pressure is well controlled on an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and her estimated glomerular filtration rate has been stable.

She has no headache today and no neurological symptoms. She has come because her mother, who had the same kidney disease, died at 52 of a bleed on the brain, and her maternal uncle had a brain aneurysm clipped in his forties. She works as a school teacher, has never smoked, and asks you directly whether she should be having a scan of her head. Her neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no papilloedema, ballotable kidneys bilaterally, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2; urine protein creatinine ratio 8 mg/mmol (less than 15)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Screening is not indicated because she has no neurological symptoms today
options.rationale: Aneurysms are asymptomatic until they bleed, so the absence of symptoms is exactly the situation in which targeted screening is worthwhile (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance angiography of the cerebral circulation now
options.rationale: A family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage or intracranial aneurysm raises the prevalence several fold and is the accepted indication for screening in this disease, with non contrast magnetic resonance angiography as the modality of choice (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography angiography and repeat it every year thereafter
options.rationale: Computed tomography angiography needs iodinated contrast and repeated radiation, and annual imaging is far more frequent than the intervals used after a negative screen (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Screening should be offered to every patient with this kidney disease routinely
options.rationale: Universal screening has not been shown to be worthwhile because the prevalence without a family history is too low to justify the anxiety and the risks of treating incidental small aneurysms (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Good blood pressure control removes the need for any imaging of her head
options.rationale: Blood pressure control reduces rupture risk and is essential, but it does not eliminate the risk conferred by the familial clustering of aneurysms (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

explanation.summary: Intracranial aneurysms occur in a minority of people with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, and they cluster strongly in families, which is why screening is targeted rather than universal. The accepted indications are a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage or intracranial aneurysm, a previous aneurysm, a high risk occupation such as a pilot, or planned major surgery or anticoagulation. Non contrast magnetic resonance angiography is preferred because it avoids radiation and iodinated contrast in a population with reduced kidney function. A negative scan is repeated at intervals of several years in those who remain at high risk, and a positive result goes to a neurosurgical or neurointerventional service, where the decision to treat weighs aneurysm size, site and morphology against the risk of the procedure. Blood pressure control and smoking cessation reduce rupture risk regardless of the imaging result.
key_points: Aneurysms cluster in families with polycystic kidney disease
Family history of haemorrhage or aneurysm is the main screening indication
Magnetic resonance angiography avoids contrast and radiation
Universal screening of all patients is not recommended
Blood pressure control and not smoking reduce rupture risk
explanation.pearls: Rescreening after a negative magnetic resonance angiogram is generally offered at intervals of about five years while the person remains high risk, rather than annually, because de novo aneurysm formation is slow.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing the biochemical workup when growth hormone excess is suspected
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old man who has come about numb hands that wake him at night. Over the past three years he has gone up two shoe sizes and has had his wedding ring cut off and enlarged twice.

His wife says he sweats through his shirt at rest and that his snoring has become much worse. He was diagnosed with hypertension last year and with impaired glucose tolerance six months ago. On examination his hands are broad with doughy soft tissue, Tinel sign is positive at both wrists, his brow and jaw are prominent, and there is a wide gap between his lower incisors. Visual field testing to confrontation is normal. He has brought photographs from a decade ago that show a strikingly different face.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 148/92, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Broad doughy hands, prominent supraorbital ridge and mandible, interdental separation, bilateral positive Tinel sign, normal confrontation visual fields
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); glycated haemoglobin 47 mmol/mol (less than 48); calcium and phosphate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 with an age matched reference range
options.rationale: This is the screening test because it reflects integrated growth hormone secretion over days rather than a moment, and it must be interpreted against age matched ranges since the normal level falls with age (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level in the morning while fasting
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with undetectable troughs in healthy people, so a single random value can be normal in disease and high in health (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation, because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around one in ten adults and would otherwise generate a false diagnosis (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

options.text: Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test with paired growth hormone sampling
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress after glucose is the confirmatory test, used when the screening result is raised or equivocal rather than as the opening investigation (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography to investigate his worsening snoring first
options.rationale: Sleep apnoea affects most patients with growth hormone excess and will need treating, but investigating it first leaves the underlying cause of the whole picture undiagnosed (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

explanation.summary: Growth hormone excess develops so gradually that patients and their families rarely notice, and the average delay from onset to diagnosis is measured in years, with the diagnosis often prompted by a dentist noticing widening interdental spaces or by old photographs. The systemic burden is what makes early diagnosis worthwhile: hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and an increased incidence of colonic polyps. The biochemical sequence runs from insulin like growth factor 1 as the screening test, to failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test as confirmation, and only then to pituitary imaging, since incidental pituitary lesions are common. Transsphenoidal surgery is the first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, a growth hormone receptor antagonist and radiotherapy for residual disease, and successful treatment reverses much of the metabolic burden.
key_points: Insulin like growth factor 1 is the screening test and needs age matched ranges
Random growth hormone levels are uninterpretable because secretion is pulsatile
Failure of suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test confirms the diagnosis
Image the pituitary only after biochemical confirmation
Screen for sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, glucose intolerance and colonic polyps
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to bring photographs from 10 and 20 years ago, because the slow change in facial soft tissue is invisible to the family who see it daily and is often the single most persuasive piece of evidence at the first consultation.

subtopic_detail: Drug treatment that must accompany resuscitation in bleeding from oesophageal varices
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 54 year old man with cirrhosis from hepatitis C has vomited a bowl of fresh blood twice in the past hour and passed a black tarry stool.

He has known oesophageal varices seen at endoscopy last year and takes propranolol. He is drowsy but rousable, with spider naevi, palmar erythema and shifting dullness. Two large bore cannulas are in, blood has gone for crossmatch, and a fluid bolus is running. The gastroenterologist has been called and says she can bring him to the endoscopy suite within the hour. His haemoglobin is 78 g/L and his international normalised ratio is 1.6.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, spider naevi, palmar erythema, shifting dullness, no asterixis, melaena on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (130-180); platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400); international normalised ratio 1.6; bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: In addition to ongoing resuscitation, what is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfuse red cells to a target haemoglobin above 100 g/L before endoscopy
options.rationale: Liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens rebleeding and mortality in this population, and a restrictive target of about 70 g/L gives better outcomes (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma to correct the international normalised ratio to below 1.5
options.rationale: The prolonged ratio in cirrhosis reflects reduced synthesis of both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors rather than a bleeding tendency, and plasma expands volume and raises portal pressure (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

options.text: Insert a balloon tamponade tube now to control bleeding before endoscopy
options.rationale: Tamponade is a rescue measure for uncontrollable bleeding, usually in an intubated patient, when endoscopy has failed or is unavailable, and endoscopy is available within the hour (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

options.text: Start terlipressin and intravenous ceftriaxone before he goes for endoscopy
options.rationale: A vasoactive drug reduces portal inflow and improves haemostasis, while antibiotic prophylaxis independently reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and mortality in cirrhotic patients bleeding from any upper gastrointestinal source (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start a high dose proton pump inhibitor infusion as the definitive drug treatment
options.rationale: Acid suppression is reasonable while the source is unknown and is continued if an ulcer is found, but it does nothing for portal pressure and is not the treatment for variceal bleeding (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

explanation.summary: Bleeding from oesophageal varices still carries a mortality of the order of 15 to 20 per cent at six weeks, and the interventions that alter that figure are given before the endoscope arrives. A vasoactive agent such as terlipressin or octreotide lowers portal inflow and is started as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected. Antibiotic prophylaxis is the intervention most often forgotten, yet it reduces infection, rebleeding and death independently, because bacterial translocation both provokes and follows the bleed. Transfusion is deliberately restrictive, aiming at around 70 g/L, because filling the circulation raises portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding. Endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours is the definitive treatment, with a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt for failure or for high risk patients, and secondary prophylaxis afterwards combines a non selective beta blocker with a banding programme.
key_points: Start a vasoactive drug as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected
Antibiotic prophylaxis reduces rebleeding and mortality independently
Transfuse restrictively to about 70 g/L rather than normalising the haemoglobin
The international normalised ratio in cirrhosis does not measure bleeding risk
Band ligation within 12 hours is the definitive endoscopic treatment
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic prophylaxis, usually intravenous ceftriaxone, is given to every cirrhotic patient with upper gastrointestinal bleeding whatever the source, and it is the omitted step most closely tied to avoidable death in this presentation.
